title: Cutting tiles with a wet tile saw
subtitle: Use a water-cooled diamond-blade tile saw to make accurate straight and rip cuts in ceramic, porcelain, and natural stone tiles
excerpt: How to use a wet tile saw to cut ceramic, porcelain, and natural stone tiles. Covers blade selection, setting up the water bath, marking tiles, making straight rip cuts and crosscuts, and cutting narrow strips safely.
sourceNotes: UK trade tiling practice and tile industry technical guidance (open access). Reader's Digest Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced).

glossaryTerms.definition: A circular saw blade with synthetic diamond particles embedded in or bonded to the rim. The diamonds abrade through hard tile and stone rather than cutting: the blade does not have teeth. A wet saw cools the blade and suppresses silica dust with a continuous water supply over the blade.

A long cut parallel to the length of the tile, used when a row of tiles must be cut down in width to fit the last row at a wall or threshold. Rip cuts on narrow strips are among the most difficult wet-saw operations because the off-cut strip can chip or bind against the blade.

content.text: A wet tile saw cuts ceramic and natural stone tiles accurately without chipping, using a water-cooled diamond blade. The blade abrades through the tile rather than cutting: feeding the tile slowly and steadily produces clean edges. BEGINNER in operation: the saw does the work; the key skill is keeping the cut line on track.
Set up the saw and fill the water reservoir
Fill the water reservoir or pan to the marked level. Check the

is the correct type for the tile material: general-purpose blades work for ceramic; hard porcelain and natural stone benefit from a blade rated for those materials. Check the blade is secure and undamaged before starting. Work on a stable surface with the run-off water draining away from electrical outlets.
Mark the cut line on the tile face with a pencil and combination square. For a straight crosscut, mark across the full width. For a

, set the saw fence or use the guide ruler, measuring and checking the distance from the blade to the fence before making the cut. Mark the offcut side so it is clear which side of the line the blade should follow.

Switch on the saw and allow the blade to reach full speed before touching the tile. Wear safety glasses. Push the tile into the blade slowly and steadily, keeping light, even forward pressure throughout. Do not force the tile: the blade should glide through with the weight of the tile providing most of the feed pressure. Keep both hands on the tile, positioned either side of the blade path but never in front of it.

Strips narrower than about 30 mm can flex or vibrate as they come off the blade. Support the off-cut strip with a finger alongside the cut line rather than behind the blade path. On very narrow strips, cut from both faces: make the first pass from the front, flip the tile and complete the cut from the other face to meet the kerf.

attrs.symptom: Chipping on the tile face at the cut line
attrs.cause: Feed pressure was too fast, the blade was blunt, or the blade type does not match the tile hardness.
attrs.fix: Slow the feed rate to a crawl. If the blade is old, replace it. For hard porcelain, use a blade rated for porcelain.

attrs.symptom: Cut wanders off the marked line mid-cut
attrs.cause: The tile shifted sideways due to insufficient pressure against the fence, or the tile was tilted during the cut.
attrs.fix: Keep the tile pressed firmly against the fence throughout the cut. For cuts without a fence, draw the cut line slightly bolder and use a slow, controlled feed.
